r-surface.$description:
The corner of a SURFACE that belongs to the page: a card, a panel, a dialog, a
sheet, a table frame. An alias of the r scale rather than a fresh number, on the same footing
as rhythm's aliases of sp, so the base value cannot drift off the radius scale.

Why the role exists at all: r names how round a corner is, and this names WHICH corner is being
asked about. A manifest that reaches for r-lg has said a length; one that reaches for r-surface
has said a reason, and only the second can be answered differently by a style plugin. Re-valuing
r-lg to soften a card would soften every unrelated use of the same step, which is the defect the
role tier exists to prevent.

r-surface-floating.$description:
The corner of a surface that floats over the page: a menu, a toast, an alert,
a bulk action bar. Separate from r-surface because the scale already separated them: r.md is
authored as "nested cards, menus" and r.lg as "cards, panels". A floating surface is smaller and
nearer the pointer, so it reads as a lighter object, and a style plugin that rounds cards without
rounding menus is the broken half-applied look this role exists to prevent.

r-control.$description:
The corner of a CONTROL the user presses: a button, an icon button, a menu item,
a pagination page, a navigation row. Separate from r-field although both are r.sm today, on the
cut that keeps rhythm-group and dz-stack apart at 12px: same length, different question. A style plugin that wants pill buttons over rectangular inputs needs the two answerable one at a time.

r-control-sm.$description:
The corner of a control too small to carry the full control radius: a checkbox
box, a segment of a segmented control. A control whose whole body is barely larger than its own
corner would read as a circle at r-control, so the scale drops a step. It is still a control, so
it moves when a style plugin moves controls, which is why this is a role and not a scale use.

r-field.$description:
The corner of a FIELD the user types into: an input, a select, a textarea.
The counterpart to r-control, and separate from it for the reason stated there.

r-marker.$description:
The corner of a MARKER: a tag, a delta badge, a keyboard cap, an inline code
chip. A marker encloses a label and nothing else. It is neither a surface, because nothing is
placed inside it, nor a control, because it cannot be pressed, and giving the family its own
role is what keeps a dozen identical exceptions out of check:roles. A marker is where a commerce
style plugin says SALE, so it earns a role rather than a frozen literal.

r-media.$description:
The corner of a MEDIA frame: the box an image, a video or a stand-in glyph is clipped to. Born at the value r-surface carries, because nothing paints a media frame until ArenaFigure does and a sibling's answer is the honest place to start from.

Separate from r-surface because the two are different questions about the same page. A card is a container the reader looks past; a figure is the thing being looked at, and a style plugin for a gallery wants its images square-cornered while its panels stay round.

aspect-media.$description:
The shape of a media frame, as the ratio of its width to its height. A number rather than a keyword, because a keyword is one bare word and a ratio is two numbers: 0.8 is the same shape as four by five, and aspect-ratio takes it. The description carries the fraction a reader recognises and the token carries the value CSS reads.

Born square, which is what the only media box in the system paints today. A style plugin for a shop wants a portrait crop, 0.8, so a product fills more of a column; a style plugin for a gallery wants the square back so a wall of them tiles.

fit-media.$description:
How the image inside a media frame meets the frame's edges. The second keyword role, and it exists for the reason the first one does: object-fit takes a word, and a manifest that writes cover has said an answer where only a question can be answered differently by one style plugin than by another.

Cover by default, which fills the frame and crops what does not fit. A style plugin that letterboxes instead is saying the whole of the image matters more than the shape of the grid, which is a coherent thing for a catalogue of artwork to say and the wrong thing for a shop.

overlay-media.$description:
The wash a media frame draws under anything laid over it, so a caption or a mark stays readable against an image nobody chose. An ASSIGNMENT like every colour role: a style plugin says which of the consumer's colours the wash takes and may not author one.

The page's own fill by default, so the wash reads as the page closing over the picture rather than as a colour of its own. The manifest carries the opacity, which is why this is a flat colour and not a translucent one: a value with alpha baked in would put the contrast floor out of reach of every gate that measures it.

fw-heading.$description:
The weight of a heading set in the display face: a card's title, a dialog's title, a
page head, a stat card's value. fw is named by VALUE, which is what makes it a scale: extrabold
is 800 whoever asked for it. This asks WHICH text is being weighted, and only a question can be
answered differently by one style plugin than by another.

It matters most to a style plugin that draws nothing. Once the boxes are gone, the distance between a
heading and the text under it IS the hierarchy, and weight is half of that distance.

track-heading.$description:
The tracking of a heading in the display face. Authored as the tight step because
that is what most title slots already reached for; the five that reached for nothing were the
inconsistency this role removes rather than a decision anybody made.

Separate from the ls steps, which are named by the thing that uses them and
are already role-shaped: a heading is the one use a style plugin has a reason to re-answer.

Carries cssUnit em like every ls step it points at: ls is authored unitless so JS can read it, and
letter-spacing needs a length. A role that forgot the unit emits a bare number, which is not a valid
letter-spacing and silently resolves to normal.

lh-prose.$description:
The leading of text somebody reads: a dialog's body, an empty state's message, a
page head's subtitle, a hint under a field. lh-root's own description already calls the three
steps below it roles rather than scale, and this names the one a style plugin has a reason to move.

It is FLOORED and not free. WCAG 1.4.8 asks 1.5 line spacing within a paragraph and technique C21
spells it out as a line-height of 1.5 on the body element, which is also exactly what lh-root is
set to. A style plugin
may open a paragraph up and may never close it below that, and check:style-plugin measures the
resolved value in every scope rather than trusting the author.

Note what is NOT the floor here: WCAG 1.4.12 is often quoted as requiring 1.5 line height, and it
does not. It requires that content survive a USER overriding spacing to those values without being
clipped or lost, which is a property of the layout and not of a token, and no gate over this file
could hold it.

lh-heading.$description:
The leading of a heading in the display face, standing opposite lh-prose: one
plugin wants a title packed and its paragraphs open, another wants both even, and the contrast
between the two IS the hierarchy on a screen where nothing is drawn.

Authored as lh.root and not as lh.snug, and the difference is the whole reason this role is safe
to add. Eight title slots reach for font-heading and exactly ONE of them declares a leading, so
seven inherit lh-root's 1.5. A role born at snug would have tightened those seven by a third of a
line the day it landed, which is a redesign wearing a refactor's clothes. It is born at what they
already compute to, and a style plugin is what moves it.

No floor, unlike lh-prose. A heading is not the text WCAG 1.4.8 is about: it is a line or two
read as a shape, and a display face set at 1.5 reads as two unrelated lines rather than as one
title.

measure-prose.$description:
How wide a column of prose is allowed to get, in ch, which is the only unit that
means anything here: a measure that does not track the font size is not a measure at all.

Carries cssUnit ch by the same mechanism ls uses for em. DTCG 2025.10 admits px and rem for a
dimension and nothing else, which is why a prose measure was once refused; the exit was that a
measure was never obliged to be a dimension. It is a number with a render hint, it widens no
conformance claim, and the reason it no longer binds is that a measure was never obliged to be
a dimension.

It reaches a page through a class a consumer applies rather than through a component slot, in
Prose.css beside Numerals.css and Rhythm.css, because the thing that wants a measure is a
document's own markup and Arena ships no prose component to hang it on. The two components that
set a measure today set 42ch and 46ch on an empty state and an error state, and those are the
width of a short blurb rather than of a reading column, so they keep their literals.

72 is where the base body size lands a line at roughly the 45 to 75 characters typography has
agreed on for a century, and check:style-plugin holds an answer inside that range.

ff-heading.$description:
Which of the three faces a heading takes. font names the family, which is what
makes the three of them the consumer's to choose; this names WHICH text is being set, so a style plugin
can answer it without owning a typeface.

Every title slot in the system reaches for the display face today, so this is born saying exactly
that. It exists because a style plugin that wanted its headings in the body face had no way to say so
without the consumer changing what the display face IS, which is a different decision entirely.

ff-eyebrow.$description:
Which face an eyebrow takes: the small line above a title that says what kind of
thing this is. All five eyebrow slots are set in the mono face, and that is a register choice
rather than a technical one, which is exactly what makes it a role.

It is the single most visible thing a style plugin can move. A console's eyebrow is a monospaced tag
reading STATUS or REGION; a shop's eyebrow reads "Single origin, Huehuetenango" and belongs in
the display face. Same slot, same size, opposite register, and before this role the difference
was unreachable from any style plugin.

ff-label.$description:
Which face the LABEL register takes: a field's label, a column header, a section
label, a group header, a badge, a keyboard cap. Born in the mono face, and that is a measurement
rather than a guess: every slot in this register is set in mono and in capitals, without one
exception across the whole system.

Split from ff-eyebrow although the two are the same face today, and the split IS the point. The
label register is a console's register and reads as the machine talking; an eyebrow is the line
above a title and reads as the page talking. A style plugin for a shop takes the eyebrow out of that
register and leaves its column headers exactly where they are, which is not expressible while
one role answers for both.

fw-eyebrow.$description:
The weight of an eyebrow. Born at fw.regular because no eyebrow slot declares a
weight at all and every one of them therefore inherits 400: the role is born at what they already
compute to, not at what would look better.

Separate from fw-control, which weights the text a user presses. An eyebrow is read and not
pressed, and a style plugin that sets its eyebrows in the display face usually wants them lighter at the
same moment it wants them larger.

fw-control.$description:
The weight of the text on a control the user presses: a button's label, a tab, a
menu item, a chip. Born at fw.semibold, which eighteen slots already spell out by name.

The fifteen slots spelling fw.bold are a second question rather than a louder answer to this one,
and they stay where they are until a style plugin asks for them: a bold slot is usually a value or a
count rather than a control, and folding the two together would make a style plugin unable to move
either without moving both.

tt-eyebrow.$description:
Whether an eyebrow is set in capitals. All five eyebrow slots are, and none of
them could say otherwise before this role, which is why every plugin's eyebrow read like a console
label however different everything around it looked.

The first keyword role in the system, and the reason the type exists: text-transform takes a word
rather than a measurement, DTCG 2025.10 types no word, and leaving it out of the token tier meant
freezing it into every manifest that paints it. The closed set is what earns the type. See
TokenTypes.md.

Capitals and tracking travel together, so a style plugin moving this almost always moves track-eyebrow with
it: the open tracking that makes capitals legible makes lowercase look sprayed.

tt-label.$description:
Whether the label register is set in capitals. Born at uppercase, which every
slot in the register already is. The first draft of this role guessed `none` from the shape of
the word `label`, and the census said otherwise: a label here is a system label, and the capitals
are what say so.

Separate from tt-eyebrow for the reason ff-label is separate from ff-eyebrow, and it is the
clearest place two style plugins disagree: a ledger keeps its column headers in capitals as a register
of record and sets its eyebrows in sentence case, and a shop does exactly the reverse.

track-eyebrow.$description:
The tracking of an eyebrow. Born at ls.label, the step all five eyebrow slots
already name.

It exists because tt-eyebrow exists and neither is much use alone. Capitals need the open
tracking to stay legible and lowercase does not want it, so a style plugin that drops the capitals and
leaves the tracking has made the line look sprayed rather than set. The pair is the decision.

Carries cssUnit em like every ls step, for the reason track-heading spells out: a bare number is not
a valid letter-spacing and resolves to normal in silence.

track-label.$description:
The tracking of a label, born at the step the field-label slots already name.
Paired with tt-label exactly as track-eyebrow is paired with tt-eyebrow, and separate from it for
the same reason: the two slots take opposite answers in the same style plugin.

step-eyebrow.$description:
Which step on the ladder an eyebrow takes. Named step and not fs because FS_STEP
already claims that prefix for the scale's own steps, and a style plugin may move those directly.

It aliases a dz step rather than an fs one, because an eyebrow is control-sized text today and
re-densifies with everything else. That alias is the reason REDECLARED_GROUPS exists in the
emitter: .arena-compact redeclares every dz step, and a role resolved at build time would have
frozen the base 11px and carried it into a compact region. It is emitted as a reference and
restated beside the density blocks, which is the same treatment a fill role gets for the same
reason one axis over.

A style plugin that moves this to an fs step takes the eyebrow OFF the density axis deliberately, which
is a coherent thing to want on a page whose eyebrow is a headline rather than a tag.

step-title-surface.$description:
Which step the title of a SURFACE takes: a card, a panel, a tile. Born at fs.h4,
which four title slots name outright.

Separate from step-title-section because the two are the hierarchy. A style plugin for a shop wants the
product name to lead its card and can raise this one alone; a style plugin for a gallery wants the title
to get out of the image's way and can lower it alone. Moving the fs ladder would have moved every
unrelated use of the same step, which is the defect the whole role tier exists to prevent.

step-title-section.$description:
Which step the title of a SECTION takes: the head of a region on a page, above
the surfaces inside it. Born at fs.h3, which the section-level title slots name today.

The cut against step-title-surface is what the title is titling, not how big it is. They happen
to be one step apart at rest, and a style plugin that widens the gap is saying the page has sections;
one that closes it is saying the page is a wall of equals.

step-title-page.$description:
Which step the title of a PAGE takes: the one heading that names the screen a
reader is on. Born at fs.h1, which is the step the page head names outright today.

It completes the ladder rather than starting one. A card's title, a section's title and a page's
title were three answers to one question, and two of them were roles while the third was a step,
so a style plugin could re-pitch a card and a section and then found the page head immovable above them.
The hierarchy a style plugin writes is the DISTANCE between these, and a rung nailed down is a hierarchy
it can only bend.

What it is not is a size for anything large. A hero's line is set by its own role, because a
landing page's opening line and the heading of a settings screen are different jobs that happen
to both be big.

step-title-hero.$description:
Which step the one line a landing page is built around takes. The fourth and last rung of the title ladder, above the page register rather than beside it: a page head names the screen a reader navigated to, and this is the sentence a page opens with.

Born at fs.display rather than at fs.hero, which is the step above it and has no consumer by design. 64 is where a hero line sits when it shares a viewport with a paragraph and two buttons; 96 is a poster, and a style plugin that wants one has the step to reach for. Being able to reach it is the point of the role.

pad-control-x.$description:
The room a CONTROL gives its content across: a button, a chip, a menu item, a tab.
Born at sp.3, the step the majority of control slots name.

The cut against dz-row-px is who is being asked about, the same cut pad-surface makes. Density
says how tight a DATA ROW is, which is target size and the same answer on a phone in any style plugin.
This says how generous a control is, which is register. A style plugin may spend it and .arena-compact
still decides the row.

pad-control-y.$description:
The room a control gives its content down. Split from pad-control-x rather than
folded into one padding role because a control's two axes are not one decision: a style plugin widens a
button without making it taller, since height is where density and target size live and width is
where air does.

gap-control.$description:
The gap between the parts of one control: an icon and its label, a checkbox and
its text, a chip and its dismiss. Born at sp.2, which nineteen slots name.

The smallest of the three air roles and the one a style plugin moves least, because it is the distance
inside a thing rather than between two things. It is here so that a style plugin which opens everything
else up does not leave its icons welded to their labels.

gap-inline.$description:
The gap between siblings sitting on one line: the actions in a toolbar, the chips
in a filter row, the items in a breadcrumb. Born at sp.2 beside gap-control, and separate from it
because the two are the difference between one control and several: a style plugin that pulls its
controls apart on a line has not said anything about what is inside them.

gap-items.$description:
The gap between the members of one group: the fields of a fieldset, the rows of a
list, the cards of a grid. Born at sp.3, which eighteen slots name.

Named items and not group, because --spacing-group is already the rhythm step. The cut is
that rhythm is air a PAGE applies between two components and
Arena never draws it, while this is air a component gives the children it lays out itself. A style
plugin usually moves both together and has to be able to move them apart, because a dense wall of
cards inside a page with generous sections is a coherent thing to want.

grid-min.$description:
The narrowest a column of an auto-fitting grid may get before the grid drops one.
Authored as a literal because it is one: ArenaGrid defaults it today to a calc of sp.1 times 50,
which is a length spelled as arithmetic rather than a step on any ladder, and 200px is what that
arithmetic produces. The card demo beside the manifest passes 136px of its own, which is a demo
choosing a narrower column and not the component default it was mistaken for once.

It is a role rather than a scale because it is the single number that decides how many cards a
viewport shows, and a gallery and a ledger want opposite answers to that from the same markup.

container-max.$description:
The widest the page's content column gets. Promoted here from spacing.json, where
it sat among the scales without being one: nothing else steps off it and no second use shares it,
so it was already a role wearing a scale's file.

It keeps its name, so --container-max and Tailwind's max-w-page are untouched by the move; what
changes is that a style plugin may now re-answer it. A style plugin for reading wants a narrower page than
a style plugin for a dashboard, and that was unreachable before.

Emitted into effects.generated.css beside the other roles rather than into spacing.generated.css,
because arena-tokens.ts reads a fixed list of four generated files and the roles all live in one
of them.

gutter.$description:
The air between the page's content column and the viewport edge. Promoted from
spacing.json with container-max and for the same reason: the two are one decision about how a
page sits, and neither is a step on a ladder anything else uses.

A style plugin moves them together. Narrowing the column while keeping the gutter says the page is a
document; widening both says it is a console.

pad-surface.$description:
The room a surface gives its own content: a card's head and body, a stat card, a
chart tile, a sign-in panel. An alias of sp on the same footing as rhythm's aliases, so the base
value cannot drift off the spacing grid.

The cut against rhythm is inside versus between: rhythm is the air BETWEEN two components, which
Arena never draws and a page applies, and this is the air a component gives its own contents.
A style plugin needs both, because a card with room inside it and none around it reads as a stripe.

The cut against density is who is being asked about. Density says how dense the CONTROLS and the
DATA ROWS are, which is target size and Fitts's law, and it is the same question on a phone in
any style plugin. This says how generous a surface is, which is a statement about the page's register.
The two compose: .arena-compact and a roomy style plugin is a coherent thing to want.

The floating tier deliberately has no role beside this one. A sheet is pinned to the viewport and
a coachmark is pinned to what it points at, so their padding is a fit constraint rather than a
statement about air, and giving a style plugin a lever there would let it push their content off the
edge. They are recorded in SCALE_USES instead.

fill-surface.$description:
The fill of a surface that belongs to the page: a card, a stat card, a table's
frame, an empty state. Arena's SECOND grouping signal and the quieter half of it, because a
region is told from the page by its edge and by its fill together.

Emitted as a reference and not as a resolved colour, which is the one place the emitter departs
from every other role: a radius resolved to 14px is right in both themes, and a colour resolved
to a hex would freeze the dark palette into the light one. A role that names WHICH step is asked
about has to keep pointing at the step rather than at what the step happens to be.

What it buys: a style plugin that groups by proximity draws nothing at all, and a fill is something
drawn. Without this role a card keeps a region the style plugin just said was not there, and the gate
holding that style plugin to its claim cannot see the fill to object. It is an ASSIGNMENT and never a
value: a style plugin may say which of the consumer's 27 colours a surface takes, and may not
author one.

fill-surface-floating.$description:
The fill of a surface that floats over the page: a menu, a dialog, a toast, a
sheet, a command palette, a bulk action bar. The same step as fill-surface today and a different
question, which is the cut r-surface and r-surface-floating already make one tier up.

This is the role that makes flattening the other one safe. A style plugin that takes a card down to the
page's own fill has said its regions are carried by air; a menu that did the same would be an
unreadable overlay, because a floating surface is separated from what it covers rather than
grouped against it. Split so a style plugin can answer the two one at a time.

fill-page.$description:
The fill of the page itself, the floor everything else stands on. What asks for it: a style
plugin that groups by marking needs to say its surfaces differ from the floor, and one that makes
its surfaces vanish needs to say they equal it. Neither sentence can be written while the floor is
a constant inside a gate instead of a role in this file.

fill-surface-sunken.$description:
The fill of a region that reads as recessed INTO a surface: a code block inside a
card, a preview well, the track a value sits in. Born at base-100, the step the one slot painting
a sunken region already names.

The third fill and the least used, and it is here because the other two cannot express it. A
sunken region is not a floating surface and not the page, and a style plugin that inverted its ramp
would otherwise have had a well that stood proud of the card containing it.

fill-field.$description:
The fill of a box the user types into: an input, a textarea, a select, the
confirmation field a destructive dialog asks for. Four slots named base-300 outright, which is
the same measurement that produced the three fills above it.

Separate from fill-surface-sunken although both are recessed today, and the split is what a
style plugin spends. A sunken region is a well inside a surface that the reader looks at; a
field is a well the reader puts a cursor in, and a plugin that makes its fields louder than its
wells is saying where the work happens. It is also the role a plugin reaches for first: a filled
field and an outlined one are the two ways any product draws a form, and before this role the
choice was unreachable.

An assignment and never a value, like every colour role. What it does NOT carry is the boundary:
bw-field and edge-field are the pair WCAG 1.4.11 measures, and this is the ground behind them.

fill-hover.$description:
The fill something takes under the pointer: an interactive table row, a card
that is a link, a secondary button, a navigation row. Four slots wrote hover:bg-base-300 by
hand, and a fifth wrote nothing at all, which is the reason this is a role rather than a step.

It is the one state every product re-decides. A dense console tints a row by one step of its own
ramp; a document tool washes it in the page's own grey; a bright product fills it with a tint of
the accent. None of those is expressible while the answer is a palette step inside a manifest,
and the measurement is that every style plugin written against Arena so far has repainted it
through a part.

Not paired with a press fill. A press is over in a hundred milliseconds and reads as the
control's own motion, which is what press-scale and lift-control are for; a hover persists and
is the surface answering.

fill-track.$description:
The ground a value runs along or a set of segments sits in, drawn as a strip
across a surface rather than as a region something is placed inside: a progress bar's track, a
segmented control's track, the head row of a table. Born at base-300, which all three slots name
outright.

Separate from fill-surface-sunken, whose own description claims a track among its uses and reaches
none: a sunken region is a well inside a surface that the reader looks at, and it is answered a
step lighter, so pointing a track at it would lighten every track and moving its answer would
darken every well. Both exits are a change of appearance dressed as a binding.

What asks for it: a style plugin that makes a bar read as a measure rather than as a control, and
one that takes the frame off a table and leaves its head row on the page. Both were measured
painting it by hand, through progress-bar.track and table.head-row.

An assignment and never a value, like every colour role: WHICH of the consumer's colours, never
what that colour is.

ink-heading.$description:
The colour of a heading. One of a hundred and twenty-two slots that pointed at
base-content directly, which is the measurement that says why the ink roles exist: a style plugin could
change every shape on the page and not one word's colour.

Split from ink-body although both are born on the same step, because that is the split a style plugin
spends. A page whose headings sit a shade above its prose reads as edited; one where they match
reads as printed, and neither is reachable while both name the palette.

An assignment and never a value, like every colour role: WHICH of the consumer's colours, never
what that colour is.

ink-body.$description:
The colour of text somebody reads. The default answer for any slot that is not a
heading, a label or muted, and the largest single group of the hundred and twenty-two.

It is where the contrast floor is enforced rather than chosen: check:text-contrast measures the
resolved level once per style plugin crossed with both themes, so a style plugin that assigns this to a step
that fails against its surface fails the build rather than the reader.

ink-eyebrow.$description:
The colour of an eyebrow. Born at primary, which four of the five eyebrow slots
name.

It is the role that lets a style plugin honour the one-primary-accent rule the SKILL.md already states.
An accent spent on every eyebrow on the page is an accent spent, and the single primary action is
what it was being saved for, so several style plugins move this to secondary for exactly that reason.
Before the role there was no way to say it.

ink-eyebrow-surface.$description:
The colour of the eyebrow of a SURFACE: a card, a dialog, a sign-in panel. Born at
primary, which is what ink-eyebrow answers, so the split moves nothing until a style plugin
moves it.

Split from ink-eyebrow on what the line is above, which is the cut step-title-surface and
step-title-section already make one tier up. An eyebrow inside a card is the card saying what kind
of thing it holds; an eyebrow over a region is the page speaking.

The one-primary-accent rule is what makes them two questions rather than one answer. An accent
spent on every card on the page is an accent spent, and the line that opens a section is what it
was being saved for, so a product holds one back and not the other. Two style plugins were
measured doing exactly that through card.eyebrow while their other eyebrows kept the accent.

A figure's frame is not in this group. It reaches for ink-eyebrow to colour the stand-in glyph
inside a media box rather than an eyebrow, and it is recorded here so its absence reads as a
decision.

An assignment and never a value, like every colour role.

ink-muted.$description:
The colour of text held back: a caption, a hint, a timestamp, a secondary line.
Born at base-content, which is what every muted slot points at today.

What it does NOT carry is the level. Fifty-nine slots write base-content at 62 percent and
thirty-one at 82, and those percentages stay in the manifests: a role names WHICH colour and the
opacity modifier is a second decision that Tailwind composes on top. So a style plugin re-points muted
text at a genuinely muted colour, and the level it is held at is unchanged.

The alternative was a role per level, which is three roles saying one thing and a style plugin unable to
move any of them without moving all three.

edge-surface.$description:
The colour of the line that encloses a surface. Standing to bw-surface exactly as
fill-surface stands to it: one says how thick the enclosure is, this says what colour it is, and
a style plugin needs both because a hairline in the page's own ramp and a hairline in neutral are two
different statements about how hard the region is.

Born at base-300, which thirty-four slots name outright. It was dropped once with the stroke
roles for want of a style plugin that asked, and those thirty-four uses are the measurement of what not
having it cost.

edge-surface-floating.$description:
The colour of the line around a surface that floats over the page. Born at
neutral, and the split from edge-surface was measured rather than designed: ten slots draw a
floating panel in neutral and ten draw a page surface in base-300, and nothing named the
difference. A floating surface sits over content rather than beside it, so its edge has to hold
against whatever is behind it.

The same cut fill-surface-floating and r-surface-floating already make, which is what says it is
a question rather than an accident. An empty state takes this edge although it does not float,
because it is a surface with nothing behind it and was already drawn at the floating strength.

edge-control-quiet.$description:
The colour of the line around a control that is present but not offering itself:
a ghost icon button, an unselected page in a pager, the track behind a segmented control, a
calendar's nav arrows. Born at base-300, which all seven such slots name.

Separate from edge-control because the difference is not a state of one control but a different
question: a quiet control's edge says where a target is without asking to be pressed. A style plugin
that wants its quiet affordances to disappear entirely, or to be exactly as hard as its active
ones, has to be able to say so without touching the boundary WCAG measures.

edge-marker.$description:
The colour of the ring around a MARKER: an avatar, a delta badge. Born at
neutral, which both slots name. The counterpart to bw-marker, and it exists for the reason that
role does: a marker is neither a surface nor a control, and without its own role a dozen
identical exceptions collect in check:roles.

A tag takes edge-surface rather than this, although a tag is a marker by radius. It is drawn as
a small panel rather than as a ring, at base-300, and it is recorded here rather than folded in
so the difference stays visible.

edge-control.$description:
The colour of the line around a control the user presses. Born at neutral, which
fifteen slots name, and separate from edge-surface because it is the boundary WCAG 1.4.11
measures at 3:1 against what sits behind it.

That is also its limit. check:boundary-contrast already measures the step behind a control whose
border a style plugin set to zero; assigning this role moves the same question onto the colour, and the
same gate answers it.

edge-field.$description:
The colour of the line around a typable field. Split from edge-control for the
reason bw-field is split from bw-control: a field is the boundary with the least freedom in the
system, because it is the one a user has to find before they can type into it.

edge-separator.$description:
The colour of the rule that divides one thing from the next inside a surface.
Born at base-300 beside edge-surface, and separate for the reason bw-separator is separate from
bw-surface: a style plugin that removes the enclosure keeps the rules, because a table whose rows lost
their lines at the same moment stops being readable.

It is the ornament a style plugin grouping by CONTINUITY would spend, if such a style plugin is ever written:
the line that runs across is the only thing saying the rows are a series.

bw-surface.$description:
The border that encloses a surface, and therefore Arena's default grouping
signal. This is the single most consequential role in the tier: a hairline says 'these things
are one region' by drawing the region, which is cheap in pixels and correct for dense data.
An style plugin that sets it to 0px has to make elevation and air carry the grouping instead,
and WCAG 1.4.11 stops being satisfied by the border, which is why removing it is gated rather
than merely allowed.

bw-control.$description:
The border of a pressable control. Distinct from bw-surface because a button's
outline is an affordance, saying where the pressable area ends, while a card's is a grouping
signal. A style plugin can drop one and keep the other.

bw-field.$description:
The border of a typable field. Distinct again: this one is the boundary WCAG
1.4.11 measures at 3:1, so it is the border with the least freedom of the three.

bw-separator.$description:
The line that divides one thing from the next INSIDE a surface: a table row
from the row under it, a sheet's head from its body, a tab strip from its panel. The critical
distinction from bw-surface, and the reason it is a separate role rather than the same one
applied to an edge: a style plugin that groups by elevation instead of by line removes the
enclosure, and a table whose rows lost their rules at the same time would stop being readable.
A separator answers a different question, so it survives the change.

bw-marker.$description:
The border of a marker, paired with r-marker for the same family and the same
reason. Also the ring an avatar draws against the surface behind it, which is a marker's border
by every property except the name.

shadow-surface-floating.$description:
The depth a surface carries AT REST because it floats over the page: a menu,
a toast, a tooltip, a bulk action bar, a card's floating variant. Distinct from the raised role
below, which is a response to a pointer rather than a statement about where a thing sits.

shadow-surface-rest.$description:
The depth a surface carries at rest when it is part of the page rather than floating
over it, which by default is none. Authored as a fully transparent shadow because DTCG 2025.10
types a shadow as offsets, blur, spread and a colour, and has no way to spell the absence of
one; a zero-size shadow at zero alpha is the same pixels and a real token.

It exists so the property is PAINTED. A token can re-value a declaration a slot already makes
and cannot add one, so a card that declared no box-shadow could never be given depth by an
extension, however the style plugin was written. This is the role that lets a style plugin trade
Arena's hairline grouping for grouping by elevation, which is the single change that separates
a console panel from a product card.

shadow-surface-deep.$description:
The depth of a surface that commands the screen, whether by covering it (a
dialog, a sheet, a command palette, a coachmark) or by being the only thing on it (the sign-in
card). Named for the tier rather than for modality, because the sign-in card is not modal and
carries the same depth for the same reason.

shadow-control-raised.$description:
What a control rises to under the pointer. The same step as a surface's raised
state today and a different question: a style plugin that lifts a call to action has no reason to
lift every card with it, and a commerce style plugin is mostly a statement about the call to action.

shadow-control-rest.$description:
The depth a control carries at rest, which by default is none, for the reason given at
shadow-surface-rest: the property has to be painted before a value can move it. A commerce
extension that gives its call to action a resting lift sets this one.

lift-control.$description:
How far a control rises under the pointer, which by default is nowhere. Declared on the
one slot that already transitions transform, so the base appearance is unchanged and an
extension has somewhere to put the gesture. Not a scale: it is a travel distance, and the
only length in the tier whose default is its own neutral rather than an alias.

dur-hover.$description:
How long a hover or press response takes. An alias of dur.fast, which is what
every such transition already spells inline. A style plugin is where motion energy is decided, and
a duration written as a scale step cannot be re-decided; written as a role it can, without
touching the transitions that are fast for a different reason.

dur-state.$description:
How long a state change the user follows takes: a switch travelling to its other
end, a progress bar reaching a new value, an onboarding dot widening to mark the step it is on.
An alias of dur.mid. Kept apart from dur-hover because the eye has to TRACK this one rather than
merely register that it happened, which is the whole reason the scale has a second step. Named
for the state and not for an entrance: every entrance in Arena is a keyframe in Animations.css,
so no manifest spells one as a duration.

ease-hover.$description:
The curve a hover or press response travels, and the other half of dur-hover: one
says how long the answer takes and this says what it feels like on the way. An alias of ease.out,
which is what every such transition already spells inline.

A duration on its own cannot carry motion character, which is why promoting only the durations
left the tier half built. Arena's default curve leaves at full speed and settles, and that reads
as an interface acknowledging a pointer the instant it arrives. A curve that starts slowly reads
as an object with mass being moved instead. Those are two style plugins making the same transition, and
only a role lets one of them be re-answered without dragging every entrance and every loop along
with it, which is exactly what re-valuing ease.out would do.

ease-state.$description:
The curve of a state change the user follows, paired with dur-state the way ease-hover
is paired with dur-hover. Kept apart from that one for the reason the two durations are kept apart:
the eye has to TRACK a switch travelling to its other end, and merely registers that a hover
happened.

No style plugin in the shipped catalogue moves it, which is the footing dur-state has stood on since the
role tier was built. It is not there in anticipation of a style plugin: it is there so a manifest that
names a state transition names a role at BOTH ends rather than a role for the duration and a scale
step for the curve, which is the split check:roles exists to refuse.

press-scale.$description:
How far a control sinks under the pointer while it is held, and the other half of
lift-control: that one says how far a control rises, this says how far it goes down. A style plugin that
gives a control mass has a reason to answer both, and until this moved out of effects.json it could
answer neither, because a scale is shared by every use that wants that value.

Authored as a literal rather than as an alias, for the reason lift-control is: neither has a scale
to alias, because nothing else in Arena travels under a pointer and nothing else compresses. Those
two are the only numbers in this tier whose value is its own.

Unitless on purpose: it is a transform scale, not a length, so it carries no dimension type and
does not re-densify. Both layers press by the same amount and each used to spell it as its own
literal -- 0.98 inline in React, scale-98 in the Tailwind manifest -- which is one design decision
written twice with nothing holding the copies in step. NOT script-readable: nothing does arithmetic
on it, both layers reference the custom property directly, and the flag is only for a value JS must
consume to produce a position.
